triage.name: COVID-19 (Coronavirus Disease 2019)
triage.reason: Common respiratory viral illness with classic fever, cough, dyspnea and anosmia; diagnosis reachable by history and testing with important pneumonia look-alikes.

demographics: Adults of any age can be affected; risk of severe disease rises steeply after age 65

In the US, hospitalization and death rates are higher among older adults and among Black, Hispanic, and American Indian/Alaska Native populations, largely reflecting exposure and access-to-care disparities

risk_factors.text: Close contact with a person known to have COVID-19
Living or working in a congregate setting (nursing home, shelter, correctional facility)
No prior vaccination or prior infection
Health care or frontline work with direct patient contact

comorbidities: Chronic lung disease (COPD, asthma, interstitial lung disease)
Heart failure or coronary artery disease
Immunosuppression (transplant, active cancer, HIV with low CD4)
social_history: Residence in a long-term care facility
Recent travel or large indoor gathering
exposures: Recent attendance at an indoor event with a known case

chief_complaints.text: I've been feeling feverish and achy since a couple of days ago
I have a cough that won't quit
I can't smell or taste anything
My throat is sore and my head is pounding
I get winded just walking to the bathroom

hpi.onset: Gradual over 1–3 days, often starting with fatigue and a scratchy throat
hpi.duration: Symptoms typically begin 2–5 days after exposure and last about 5–10 days in mild illness
hpi.progression: Builds over the first few days; fever and cough peak around days 3–5. Most people improve by day 7–10. A minority worsen around days 5–10 with increasing breathlessness and low oxygen, which is the window for severe disease
hpi.location: Upper airway and chest; body-wide aching
hpi.quality: Dry or minimally productive cough; burning sore throat; deep muscle aches; frontal or global headache
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate in most; can become severe with marked dyspnea and hypoxia
hpi.timing: Continuous, with fever spiking in the late afternoon and evening
aggravating: Lying flat when short of breath

associated_symptoms.text: New loss of smell or taste

pertinent_negatives: Productive cough with thick colored sputum
Pleuritic chest pain that is sharp and one-sided
Sudden onset of symptoms within minutes to hours
Sneezing and itchy watery eyes as the main problem
Known close contact with someone who has influenza or RSV

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with confusion, falls, poor appetite, or worsening of a chronic condition rather than fever and cough; hypoxia can be present with few symptoms.

Often mild or asymptomatic; when symptomatic, may have fever, cough, sore throat, and GI upset. Rarely develop a post-infectious inflammatory syndrome with persistent fever, rash, conjunctivitis, and abdominal pain.
May have prolonged viral shedding, atypical or blunted symptoms, and higher risk of severe pneumonia despite fewer initial symptoms.
Higher risk of severe disease and preterm birth; symptoms may overlap with normal pregnancy complaints like shortness of breath and fatigue.

general.mild: Alert, well-appearing, speaking in full sentences; may look tired or flushed
general.moderate: Mildly ill-appearing, slightly breathless when talking or moving around the exam room
general.severe: Ill-appearing, diaphoretic, speaking in short phrases, sitting upright and leaning forward to breathe
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, agitated or somnolent, using accessory muscles, may be unable to speak in full sentences

findings.maneuver: Measure temperature and ask about subjective fever and chills
findings.finding: Documented fever or history of fever with chills

findings.maneuver: Count the respiratory rate for a full minute at rest
findings.finding: Respiratory rate above 20/min

findings.maneuver: Place a pulse oximeter on the finger and record the reading
findings.finding: Oxygen saturation below 94% on room air

findings.maneuver: Observe the patient's breathing at rest
findings.finding: Use of accessory muscles of respiration, nasal flaring, or intercostal retractions

findings.maneuver: Auscultate all lung fields with the patient breathing deeply through the mouth
findings.finding: Diffuse bilateral crackles or rales, often at the bases
Clear breath sounds without crackles, wheezes, or focal dullness

findings.maneuver: Percuss and auscultate for focal dullness with egophony or bronchial breath sounds
findings.finding: No focal consolidation signs

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to identify a familiar scent or taste, or ask directly about loss of smell and taste
findings.finding: Reduced or absent sense of smell and/or taste

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oropharynx with a light and tongue blade
findings.finding: Mild diffuse pharyngeal erythema without exudate or asymmetry

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oropharynx and palpate the neck
findings.finding: No tonsillar exudate, uvular deviation, or unilateral swelling

findings.maneuver: Palpate the radial pulse or auscultate the heart
findings.finding: Heart rate above 100/min

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart at the apex and base
findings.finding: Regular rate and rhythm without murmurs, rubs, or gallops

findings.maneuver: Inspect the neck veins and press on the shins for pitting edema
findings.finding: No jugular venous distension and no peripheral edema

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation to person, place, and time and ask about confusion
findings.finding: New confusion or disorientation, especially in older adults

findings.maneuver: Test strength, sensation, and speech, and check for neck stiffness
findings.finding: No focal weakness, sensory loss, slurred speech, or meningismus

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin, including the toes, for rash or discoloration
findings.finding: No petechiae, diffuse erythroderma, or new rash

labs.caveat: Lymphopenia is a common early finding and supports a viral cause; it is not specific.
Often normal or low; marked leukocytosis suggests bacterial superinfection or another diagnosis.
Mild thrombocytopenia is common; a falling count with rising D-dimer raises concern for severe coagulopathy.
Rises with inflammation; a high or rising value supports severe disease but does not distinguish viral from bacterial.
Nonspecific marker of tissue injury; adds to severity assessment.
Markedly elevated ferritin with high CRP and low platelets raises concern for a hyperinflammatory state.
Often elevated from inflammation alone; a very high value with worsening hypoxia should prompt evaluation for pulmonary embolism.
Mild transaminitis is common and usually resolves; marked elevation suggests another cause.
Rising creatinine in severe disease reflects dehydration, acute kidney injury, or multiorgan involvement.
Mild hyponatremia can occur with severe illness.
Elevation suggests myocardial injury; check in severe disease or with chest pain, ECG changes, or hemodynamic instability.
A low value argues against bacterial coinfection; a high value should prompt a search for bacterial superinfection.
Elevated lactate with hypotension or hypoperfusion marks critical illness.
Early disease often shows a low CO2 from hyperventilation; a rising CO2 signals impending respiratory failure.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia
Sinus bradycardia can occur, sometimes in otherwise stable patients
Diffuse ST elevation or depression with PR depression suggesting myopericarditis
Diffuse T-wave inversions or flattening
New bundle branch block or atrioventricular block
Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response

findings.text: Normal or no acute cardiopulmonary process
Bilateral patchy or hazy opacities, often peripheral and basilar
Focal lobar consolidation suggesting bacterial superinfection

imaging.preferred_when: When the diagnosis is uncertain, another cause is suspected, or complications are being evaluated

findings.text: Crazy-paving pattern with interlobular septal thickening
Pulmonary embolism (filling defect in pulmonary arteries) when CT angiography is performed

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected pulmonary embolism (sudden worsening hypoxia, pleuritic pain, high D-dimer)

findings.text: Filling defect in one or more pulmonary arteries
Right ventricular enlargement with interventricular septal bowing

imaging.preferred_when: Bedside assessment of hypoxia when transport is limited

findings.text: Bilateral B-lines in a patchy distribution

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected myocarditis, heart failure, or hemodynamic instability

findings.text: Global or regional left ventricular dysfunction

initial.why: Looks for lymphopenia, leukocytosis, and thrombocytopenia
Assesses hydration, kidney function, and electrolytes
Baseline inflammatory marker that helps gauge severity
Fast bedside test when symptoms are present; a negative result in a high-risk patient needs a molecular test
Most sensitive test to confirm infection

initial.only_if: hypoxia, abnormal lung exam, or suspected pneumonia

decision_points: A negative rapid antigen test does not rule out COVID-19 when suspicion is high; confirm with a molecular test
Pulse oximetry below 94% on room air marks moderate or worse disease and changes disposition
Sudden worsening hypoxia or pleuritic chest pain should prompt evaluation for pulmonary embolism
Chest pain with ECG changes or troponin elevation should prompt evaluation for myocarditis or myocardial infarction
New confusion in an older adult is a red flag for severe disease even without fever or cough

criteria.name: SARS-CoV-2 infection categories (paraphrased)
criteria.summary: Confirmed infection requires a positive molecular or antigen test. Severity is classified by symptoms and oxygen needs: mild illness without hypoxia; moderate illness with lower respiratory involvement and oxygen saturation at or above 94% on room air; severe illness with oxygen saturation below 94%, respiratory rate at or above 30/min, or lung infiltrates involving more than half the lung fields; critical illness with respiratory failure, shock, or multiorgan dysfunction.
items: Mild: no hypoxia or lower respiratory symptoms
Moderate: lower respiratory symptoms with oxygen saturation at or above 94% on room air
Severe: oxygen saturation below 94% on room air, respiratory rate at or above 30/min, or extensive lung infiltrates
Critical: respiratory failure, shock, or multiorgan dysfunction

differential.name: Influenza
differential.why_considered: Fever, myalgias, sore throat, cough, and headache are nearly identical to COVID-19, and both circulate in the same seasons.

history: Abrupt onset over hours rather than 1–3 days
Prominent myalgias and high fever at the start
Loss of smell or taste is uncommon
Known influenza exposure or circulating influenza in the community
exam: Similar: fever, pharyngeal erythema, clear lungs
labs: Lymphopenia can occur but is less characteristic
imaging: Chest x-ray usually normal in uncomplicated disease

differential.name: Respiratory syncytial virus infection
differential.why_considered: Cough, congestion, sore throat, and low-grade fever, especially in older adults and young children.

history: Prominent nasal congestion and wheezing
Gradual onset without prominent myalgias
Loss of smell or taste is uncommon
imaging: Chest x-ray usually normal or with hyperinflation

differential.name: Bacterial community-acquired pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Fever, cough, and dyspnea with hypoxia can look identical, and bacterial superinfection can complicate COVID-19.
differential.trigger: Focal consolidation on exam or imaging, productive cough with colored sputum, or marked leukocytosis

history: Productive cough with thick colored sputum
Pleuritic chest pain that is sharp and one-sided
Sudden onset rather than gradual
No loss of smell or taste
exam: Focal dullness, egophony, or bronchial breath sounds
Focal crackles rather than diffuse bilateral crackles
imaging: Focal lobar consolidation on chest x-ray or CT

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: Sudden worsening dyspnea and hypoxia with chest discomfort can mimic severe COVID-19, and COVID-19 itself increases thromboembolic risk.
differential.trigger: Sudden worsening hypoxia, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, or a very high D-dimer

history: Sudden onset of dyspnea rather than gradual worsening
Pleuritic chest pain and hemoptysis
Recent immobility, surgery, or known malignancy
No fever or anosmia
exam: Signs of right heart strain such as jugular venous distension or a loud P2
Unilateral leg swelling suggesting deep vein thrombosis
labs: Elevated troponin or NT-proBNP from right heart strain
imaging: Filling defect in pulmonary arteries on CT pulmonary angiography
Right ventricular enlargement with septal bowing

differential.name: Myocarditis
differential.why_considered: Chest pain, dyspnea, and fatigue with troponin elevation can occur in COVID-19 and in other viral infections.
differential.trigger: Chest pain with ECG changes or troponin elevation

history: Chest pain at rest or with exertion
Palpitations or syncope
Recent viral illness
Less prominent cough and anosmia
exam: Tachycardia out of proportion to fever
New murmur, gallop, or signs of heart failure
labs: Negative SARS-CoV-2 molecular test if another virus is the cause
imaging: Global or regional left ventricular dysfunction on echocardiogram
Late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI
ecg: Diffuse ST elevation or depression with PR depression
New bundle branch block or atrioventricular block

differential.name: Allergic rhinitis
differential.why_considered: Nasal congestion, sore throat, and cough can be mistaken for mild COVID-19.

history: Sneezing and itchy watery eyes as the main problem
No fever or myalgias
Recurrent seasonal pattern
No loss of smell or taste

differential.name: Post-COVID conditions (long COVID)
differential.why_considered: Persistent fatigue, brain fog, dyspnea, and cough after a COVID-19 illness can be confused with ongoing acute infection.

history: Symptoms lasting weeks to months after the acute illness
No fever or acute worsening
Often after a documented prior infection
imaging: Chest imaging usually normal or with residual scarring

severity.mild: Upper airway and constitutional symptoms without lower respiratory involvement or hypoxia; oxygen saturation at or above 94% on room air; able to manage at home
severity.moderate: Lower respiratory involvement with cough and dyspnea but oxygen saturation at or above 94% on room air; may need monitoring and supportive care
severity.severe: Oxygen saturation below 94% on room air, respiratory rate at or above 30/min, or lung infiltrates involving more than half the lung fields; requires hospitalization and oxygen
severity.critical: Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, shock, or multiorgan dysfunction; requires intensive care

red_flags.finding: Oxygen saturation below 94% on room air
red_flags.meaning: Moderate or worse disease; changes disposition and need for oxygen
Impending respiratory failure; needs urgent evaluation

red_flags.finding: New confusion or disorientation, especially in an older adult
red_flags.meaning: Severe disease even without fever or cough; assess oxygenation and consider other causes

red_flags.finding: Sudden worsening hypoxia or pleuritic chest pain
Chest pain with ECG changes or troponin elevation

red_flags.meaning: Shock or sepsis; needs immediate resuscitation

complications.name: Post-COVID conditions (long COVID)
clues: Fatigue, brain fog, dyspnea, or cough lasting weeks to months after the acute illness
Symptoms not explained by another cause

special_populations.differences: May present with confusion, falls, poor appetite, or worsening of a chronic condition rather than fever and cough; hypoxia can be present with few symptoms, and risk of severe disease rises steeply after age 65.

Often mild or asymptomatic; when symptomatic, may have fever, cough, sore throat, and GI upset. Rarely develop a post-infectious inflammatory syndrome with persistent fever, rash, conjunctivitis, and abdominal pain.
May have prolonged viral shedding, atypical or blunted symptoms, and higher risk of severe pneumonia despite fewer initial symptoms.
Higher risk of severe disease and preterm birth; symptoms may overlap with normal pregnancy complaints like shortness of breath and fatigue.
Higher risk of severe disease and need for hospitalization; may have baseline dyspnea and reduced functional reserve.
Higher risk of severe disease and complications; glucose control may worsen during illness.

key_questions.question: When did your symptoms start, and how have they changed since then?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over 1–3 days; worsening breathlessness around days 5–10 suggests severe disease

key_questions.question: Have you been in close contact with anyone who has COVID-19, or been in a crowded indoor setting without a mask?
key_questions.looking_for: Household member, workplace outbreak, or indoor gathering with a known case

key_questions.question: Have you lost your sense of smell or taste?
key_questions.looking_for: New loss of smell or taste strongly supports COVID-19 over other viral illnesses

key_questions.question: Do you have a fever, chills, or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever with chills, often spiking in the late afternoon and evening

key_questions.question: Are you coughing? Is it dry or are you bringing anything up?
key_questions.looking_for: Dry or minimally productive cough; thick colored sputum suggests bacterial superinfection

key_questions.question: Are you short of breath? Does it happen at rest or only with exertion?
key_questions.looking_for: Dyspnea at rest or with minimal exertion marks moderate or worse disease

key_questions.question: How far can you walk before you have to stop and catch your breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Declining exercise tolerance; walking to the bathroom and getting winded is a red flag

key_questions.question: Do you have any muscle aches, headache, or sore throat?
key_questions.looking_for: Common constitutional symptoms supporting a viral syndrome

key_questions.question: Any nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: GI symptoms sometimes occur and can be the presenting complaint

key_questions.question: Have you had any chest pain or palpitations?
key_questions.looking_for: Pleuritic pain or chest pressure raises concern for pulmonary embolism or myocarditis

key_questions.question: Have you been confused or had trouble concentrating?
key_questions.looking_for: New confusion, especially in older adults, is a red flag for severe disease

key_questions.question: Have you been vaccinated against COVID-19, and when was your last dose or prior infection?
key_questions.looking_for: No prior vaccination or infection increases risk of severe disease

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, lung disease, heart disease, kidney disease, or a weakened immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Comorbidities that raise the risk of severe disease and change disposition

key_questions.question: Do you take any medications that suppress the immune system, like prednisone or tacrolimus?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunosuppressive medications increase risk of severe or prolonged disease

key_questions.question: Do you live in a nursing home, shelter, or other group setting?
key_questions.looking_for: Congregate living increases exposure risk and risk of severe disease

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy increases risk of severe disease and preterm birth

reasoning_points: Gradual onset over 1–3 days of fever, dry cough, fatigue, and myalgias
New loss of smell or taste strongly supports COVID-19 over other viral illnesses
Close contact with a known case or indoor crowded gathering without masks
Risk factors such as age 65 or older, obesity, diabetes, chronic lung or kidney disease, or immunosuppression
Hypoxia with oxygen saturation below 94% on room air marks moderate or worse disease
Negative rapid antigen test does not rule out COVID-19 when suspicion is high; confirm with a molecular test
Sudden worsening hypoxia or pleuritic chest pain should prompt evaluation for pulmonary embolism
Chest pain with ECG changes or troponin elevation should prompt evaluation for myocarditis or myocardial infarction

easy: Young or middle-aged adult with fever, dry cough, myalgias, and new loss of smell or taste
Known household contact with confirmed COVID-19
Clear lungs with normal oxygen saturation
medium: Older adult with fever and cough but no loss of smell
Patient with chronic lung disease and baseline dyspnea
Mild hypoxia with oxygen saturation 90–94% on room air
Negative rapid antigen test requiring molecular confirmation
hard: Older adult presenting with confusion or a fall without fever or cough
Immunocompromised patient with blunted or atypical symptoms and prolonged shedding
Pregnant patient with dyspnea overlapping normal pregnancy complaints
Sudden worsening hypoxia suggesting pulmonary embolism
Chest pain with ECG changes or troponin elevation suggesting myocarditis
